title: (Sliced) Wasserstein - Gaussian process regression workflow
text: Let’s load slicer. generate input distributions, define generate_data(): plots show two empirical distributions, using rotation angle ω=π/16\omega = \pi/16 using one ω=3π/8\omega = 3\pi/8.
code: library(slicer) generate_data <- function(n = 200, a = 5, angle = 0, Sigma = diag(1, 2)) {   mus <- cbind(c(a, 0), c(0, a), c(-a, 0), c(0, -a))   R <- rbind(     c(cos(angle), -sin(angle)),     c(sin(angle), cos(angle))   )   cluster <- sample(1:4, size = n, replace = TRUE)   d <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = 2)   for (i in 1:4) {     d[which(cluster == i), ] <- MASS::mvrnorm(       sum(cluster == i), mu = mus[, i], Sigma = Sigma     )   }   d %*% t(R) } set.seed(2026) # for reproducibility  op <- par(no.readonly = TRUE, bty = "n") par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) generate_data(angle = pi/16) |>    plot(xlab = "first dimension", ylab = "second dimension", asp = 1) generate_data(angle = 3*pi/8) |>    plot(xlab = "first dimension", ylab = "second dimension", asp = 1) par(op)

title: (Sliced) Wasserstein - Gaussian process regression workflow
text: generate 60 matrices (40 training, 20 testing) containing empirical distributions rotation angles sampled uniformly [0,π/4)[0, \pi/4). empirical distribution based 200 data points.
code: sample_size <- 200 N_train <- 40 N_test  <- 20 angle_range <- c(0, pi/4)  angles <- runif(N_train + N_test, angle_range[1], angle_range[2])  distributions <- vector("list", N_train + N_test) for (i in seq_len(N_train + N_test)) {   distributions[[i]] <- generate_data(angle = angles[i]) }

title: (Sliced) Wasserstein - Gaussian process regression workflow
text: can use compute_all_distances() compute pairwise distances input distributions. supply optional vector test_idx test set indices, pairwise distance computations test objects (needed obtaining predictions) skipped. compute sliced Wasserstein distances, need first generate 𝛉𝟏,…,𝛉𝐋\boldsymbol{\theta_1}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta_L} sampled uniformly random unit sphere; generate_directions() takes care . ’ll use L=25L = 25 set d=2d = 2 since ’re working two dimensions. ’re interested estimated sliced Wasserstein distances, can set keep_projections FALSE. 60×6060 \times 60 matrix sw_distances contains squared (estimated) sliced Wasserstein distances among forty training objects training objects twenty test objects. pairwise distances among test objects set NA: can also compute (normal) Wasserstein distances distributions projected along certain dimensions. instances, compute pairwise Wasserstein distances along first margin along second margin, set projection directions 𝐞𝟏=(1,0)⊤\boldsymbol{e_1} = (1, 0)^{\top} 𝐞𝟐=(0,1)⊤\boldsymbol{e_2} = (0, 1)^{\top}. also set keep_projections = TRUE, cause function output list two matrices squared Wasserstein distances: one margin.
code: thetas <- generate_directions(L = 25, d = 2) sw_distances <- compute_all_distances(distributions, thetas, verbose = FALSE,     keep_projections = FALSE, test_idx = N_train + seq_len(N_test)) sw_distances # output not shown marginal_distances <- compute_all_distances(distributions, diag(1, 2),      verbose = FALSE, keep_projections = TRUE,      test_idx = N_train + seq_len(N_test)) str(marginal_distances) #> List of 2 #>  $ : num [1:60, 1:60] 0 1.274 0.931 0.548 0.649 ... #>  $ : num [1:60, 1:60] 0 2.177 0.121 0.445 0.599 ...

what: Wasserstein distances between univariate empirical distributions
title: How to compute Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein distances
text: Let’s first load slicer package set random seed. Given two empirical distributions ℝ\mathbb{R}, P=1m∑=1mδxiP = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{=1}^m \delta_{x_i} Q=1n∑j=1nδyj,Q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \delta_{y_j}, want compute Wasserstein distance order p∈[1,∞)p \[1, \infty). defined 𝐖p(P,Q):=minX∼PY∼Q(𝔼|X−Y|p)1/p.\mathbf{W}_p(P, Q) := \min_{\substack{X \sim P \\ Y \sim Q}} \left(\mathbb{E}|X - Y|^p\right)^{1/p}. distributions PP QQ represented vectors (matrices) x=(x1,…,xm)∈ℝm×1x = (x_1, \dots, x_m) \\mathbb{R}^{m \times 1} y=(y1,…,yn)∈ℝn×1y = (y_1, \dots, y_n) \\mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}, respectively. instance, north-west corner algorithm used compute exact Wasserstein distances order pp. function nw_corner_distance() runs . algorithm essentially sorting operation bells whistles. working large presorted vectors, can set parameter value presorted TRUE speed-. Typically, several empirical distributions P1,…,PNP_1, \dots, P_N. function compute_all_distances() takes list empirical distributions represented vectors (matrices). don’t specify anything contrary, assume input distributions univariate. default, outputs pairwise pp-Wasserstein distances raised pp-th_power. (reason , practice, often ) Also default, p=2p = 2 used. actual 𝐖2\mathbf{W}_2 distances can now obtain taking square root: Different orders (pp) can specified, :

title: How to compute Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein distances
text: possible define Wasserstein distances dd-dimensinal distributions d≥2d \geq 2, distances expensive compute. Moreover, Hilbertian. However, can define number vectors θ1,…,θL∈ℝd\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L \\mathbb{R}^d compute pp-Wasserstein distances projections distributions onto vectors. precisely, let P1,…,PNP_1, \dots, P_N dd-dimensional empirical distributions let θ1,…,θL\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L projection vectors ℝd\mathbb{R}^d. now compute 𝐖p(θℓ#⋆Pi,θℓ#⋆Pj)\mathbf{W}_p({\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_i, {\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_j) ℓ=1,…,L,1≤<j≤N\ell = 1, \dots, L, 1 \leq < j \leq N, v#⋆Qv_{\#}^{\star}Q pushforward (image) measure QQ map x↦v⊤xx \mapsto v^{\top}x. Using slicer, can compute L⋅N(N−1)/2L \cdot N(N-1)/2 pairwise distances follows. represent dd-dimensional empirical distribution Pi=1ni∑k=1niδxi,k,P_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{k = 1}^{n_i} \delta_{x_{, k}}, xi,k∈ℝdx_{,k} \\mathbb{R}^d, matrix, Mi=(xi,1⊤⋮xi,ni⊤)∈ℝni×d.M_i =  \begin{pmatrix}   x^{\top}_{, 1} \\   \vdots \\   x^{\top}_{, n_i} \end{pmatrix} \\mathbb{R}^{n_i \times d}. put matrices M1,…,MNM_1, \dots, M_N list. , define matrix Θ=(θ1⊤⋮θL⊤)∈ℝL×d\Theta = \begin{pmatrix} \theta^{\top}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta^{\top}_L \end{pmatrix} \\mathbb{R}^{L \times d} contains projection vectors. ’re just interested obtaining Wasserstein distances corresponding marginal distributions, set Θ=Id\Theta = I_d. , feed list MM-matrices Θ\Theta compute_all_distances(). way example, Todo: Example GMMs.
code: rgmm_random <- function(n, C, r) {   p <- sample.int(C, 1)    mu <- matrix(runif(p * r, -5, 5), nrow = p, ncol = r)   chol_list <- lapply(seq_len(p), function(j) {     a <- runif(1, 1, 4)     A <- matrix(runif(r * r, -1, 1), r, r)     B <- diag(runif(r, 0, 1), nrow = r)     Sigma <- a * tcrossprod(A) + B     chol(Sigma)          })   z <- sample.int(p, n, replace = TRUE)   X <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = r)   for (j in seq_len(p)) {     idx <- which(z == j)     m <- length(idx)     if (m > 0) {       Z <- matrix(rnorm(m * r), m, r)       X[idx, ] <- Z %*% chol_list[[j]] +         matrix(mu[j, ], m, r, byrow = TRUE)     }   }   list(distribution = X, components = p) } rgmm_random_T <- function(N = 100, n = 50, C = 2, r = 2) {   replicate(N, rgmm_random(n, C, r), simplify = FALSE) }

title: Pairwise Wasserstein Distances Along Projection Directions Between Several Empirical Distributions — compute_all_distances
text: Wasserstein distance order p = 2 well square root Wasserstein distance order p = 1 Hilbertian distances univariate probability distributions. Similarly, sliced Wasserstein distance order p = 2 well square root sliced Wasserstein distance order p = 1 Hilbertian distances multivariate distributions. can therefore slot distances Gaussian radial basis function obtain valid kernel. Downstream, workflow simplified somewhat compute_all_distances() return raw Wasserstein distances p-Wasserstein p-sliced Wasserstein distances raised p-th power. way, squared (sliced) 2-Wasserstein distances can directly fed , say, rbf() default parameter setting squared = TRUE, can raw (sliced) 1-Wasserstein distances. text: Kxx Kernel matrix evaluated training inputs. Kxstar Matrix kernel values test training inputs. row corresponds one test input. y_train Vector training outcomes. centre TRUE (defaults), training outcomes centred around mean. lambda2 Kernel noise variance. Kxstarstar Optional. square matrix kernel values among test inputs. NULL (default), posterior means computed returned vector. Else posterior mean vector covariance matrix returned.

title: Predict Outcomes Using Gaussian Process Regression — gpr_predict
text: Kxstarstar NULL (default), vector posterior mean predictions test inputs. Else, list vector test_predictions posterior mean predictions matrix test_variance posterior covariance test inputs.

title: Predict Outcomes Using Gaussian Process Regression — gpr_predict
code: N1 <- 25 N2 <- 10 x_train <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = N1) x_test  <- runif(N2, -pi, pi) distance <- outer(c(x_train, x_test), c(x_train, x_test), "-") |> abs() kernel <- rbf(distance, length_scale = 1, variance = 1) Kxx    <- kernel[1:N1, 1:N1] Kxstar <- kernel[(N1+1):(N1+N2), 1:N1] Kxstarstar <- kernel[(N1+1):(N1+N2), (N1+1):(N1+N2)] y_train <- ifelse(x_train == 0, 2*pi, sin(2*pi*x_train) / x_train) curve(sin(2*pi*x)/x, from = -pi, to = pi) points(x_train, y_train) # Only means: don't use Kxstarstar points(x_test, gpr_predict(Kxx, Kxstar, y_train), pch = 16) # Add credible intervals around predictions: gpr_fit <- gpr_predict(Kxx, Kxstar, y_train, Kxstarstar = Kxstarstar) segments(x0 = x_test,          y0 = gpr_fit$test_predictions - 2 * sqrt(diag(gpr_fit$test_variance)),          y1 = gpr_fit$test_predictions + 2 * sqrt(diag(gpr_fit$test_variance)), col = "#4DAF4A")

text: fit Gaussian process model fit obtained gpr_predict() fit_gpr(). y_test vector true test outcomes. add_noise TRUE (default), y_test assumed noisy observation noise added variance posterior covariance. nugget Numeric; base jitter added covariance diagonal needed ensure positive definiteness. title: Negative Log Predictive Density for Gaussian Process Regression Models — nlpd_gpr
code: set.seed(2026-06-25) N1 <- 50 N2 <- 20 x_train <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = N1) x_test  <- runif(N2, -pi, pi) y_train <- x_train * plogis(x_train) * cos(x_train) + rnorm(N1, sd = 0.5) y_test <- x_test * plogis(x_test) * cos(x_test) D2 <- outer(c(x_train, x_test), c(x_train, x_test), "-")^2 fit <- fit_gpr(D2, seq_len(N1), N1 + seq_len(N2), y_train, y_test,                runs = 20L, cores = 1) #> Hyperparameter search 1 of 20. #> Optimum set at 65.1049. #> Hyperparameter search 2 of 20. #> Current optimum improved from 65.1049 to 65.1049. #> Hyperparameter search 3 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 4 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 5 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 6 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 7 of 20. #> Current optimum improved from 65.1049 to 65.1049. #> Hyperparameter search 8 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 9 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 10 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 11 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 12 of 20. #> Current optimum improved from 65.1049 to 65.1049. #> Hyperparameter search 13 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 14 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 15 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 16 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 17 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 18 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 19 of 20. #> Hyperparameter search 20 of 20. # noisy outcome nlpd_gpr(fit, y_test + rnorm(N2, sd = 0.5)) #> [1] 1.424344 #> attr(,"jitter_used") #> [1] 0 # clean outcome nlpd_gpr(fit, y_test, add_noise = FALSE) #> [1] 1.249706 #> attr(,"jitter_used") #> [1] 0
